dashboard.about.faq_a1: It displays the live Hebrew date, time, weather, and days of the week for use on classroom SmartBoards or projectors during morning routine and Hebrew instruction.

fontmaker.about.faq_a_commercial: That depends on the license you pick when you export. CC0 places the font in the public domain — free for any use, including commercial, with no attribution required. OFL and MIT are also free for commercial use under their terms. All Rights Reserved keeps the font yours to license as you wish. You own what you create; IvritSuite claims no rights to your fonts.
fontmaker.about.faq_a_formats: TrueType (TTF), WOFF2 for the web, and editable UFO source — each with a license you choose (CC0, OFL, MIT, or All Rights Reserved).
fontmaker.about.faq_a_free: Yes. The Hebrew Font Maker is completely free — make and download as many Hebrew fonts as you like, with no account or sign-up.
fontmaker.about.faq_a_how: Upload or scan a picture of each Hebrew letter — or draw it right in the browser — then trace it into an outline, place the nikkud and trop anchors, and export a real font you can install.
fontmaker.about.faq_a_install: On Windows, double-click the downloaded .ttf file and choose Install. On Mac, double-click it and click Install Font in Font Book. Google Docs only uses fonts from its own catalog and cannot load a local font, so use a desktop word processor such as Word, Pages, or LibreOffice, or upload the file to a design tool like Canva instead.
fontmaker.about.faq_a_marks: Yes. As you build each letter you can anchor its nikkud and trop marks, and the exported font uses OpenType GPOS mark positioning so the marks land in the right place automatically as you type. You can also make a letters-only font and skip the marks.
fontmaker.about.faq_a_nikkudtrop: Yes. The free Hebrew Font Maker positions nikkud (vowels) and cantillation (trop) automatically using OpenType mark positioning.
fontmaker.about.faq_a_software: No. The Hebrew Font Maker runs entirely in your browser; the font engine loads only when you export.

fontmaker.about.footer_about_body: A free, experimental IvritSuite tool. Builds real fonts entirely client-side (the font engine loads on first export), with GPOS mark positioning for nikkud (mark-to-base) and cantillation/trop (mark-to-mark). Exports TrueType (TTF), WOFF2 and editable UFO source.

fontmaker.changelog.v1_1: v1.1 — Import an existing TTF's letter outlines, its own nikkud & trop mark shapes, and its real anchor positions — so you can fix or build on existing fonts. Exported fonts now embed the license name and a Made-with-IvritSuite attribution in their metadata. Bigger editing workspace on wide monitors. Removed the CC BY 4.0 license option. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v1_2: v1.2 — Size the dagesh dot and the holam on the vav (וֹ) each on their own, separate from the vowels — the standalone holam now matches the hiriq — and fine-tune any single vowel's height to line it up with the rest. Prepositive & postpositive trop (telisha gedola, yetiv, pashta, zarqa, zinor, telisha qetana) now sit toward the leading or trailing edge of their letter, the way the tradition places them. Your work is auto-saved in this browser — reopen and continue right where you left off, with a warning before you close unsaved changes. A new quality check flags outlines that cross or overlap themselves. Accessibility: full keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, status badges that don't rely on color alone, reduced-motion support, and dark mode that follows your device. Zoom now centers on the middle of the workspace. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v1_3: v1.3 — Placing nikkud & trop now works like the rest of the tool: your moves apply live and you can leave a letter freely — no save dialog — with undo as the safety net. The grid now tells confirmed placements apart from ones carried over from the previous letter: a solid green ✓ means you reviewed it, a hollow amber ✓ means "carried over — review & confirm", and amber ! means unconfirmed. "Save Placement" is now an optional ✓ Confirm placement review marker. The step tabs show a per-letter checklist (✓ done / ✗ to-do / – not needed) for the letter you're on. The toolbar is now grouped — Project · History · Review · Export — with Export the clear primary action and Help moved up to the top corner. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v1_4: v1.4 — A new Edit shape editor lets you redesign any nikkud, dagesh, or trop mark from simple dots and bars — round or square dots, square or rounded bars — then apply your shape to the current letter or to all letters. Position each dot or bar by dragging it, nudging with the arrow keys, or typing exact X / Y coordinates — and set a dot's radius or a bar's width & height — for pixel-perfect placement; Reset restores a mark's default shape, and undo / redo (Ctrl/Cmd+Z) covers every change in the editor. The on-stage selection box hugs the mark's actual shape so a small or square mark is never hidden under the handle. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v1_5: v1.5 — Trop marks can now sit Left, Center, or Right of a letter, not just above or below — so each cantillation mark lands on the correct part of the glyph and look-alikes (e.g. Yetiv vs. Mahpakh, Geresh vs. Geresh Muqdam) read correctly. Every mark has a sensible default side (Segol, Zarqa, Pashta & Telisha Qetana go left; Geresh Muqdam, Deḥi, Yetiv & Telisha Gedola go right; the rest stay centered) that you can change per mark in Place Trop, with a Default spread slider for how far the side marks shift. Need a custom position on one letter? Just drag the mark (or type exact X / Y) to override that letter alone. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v1_6: v1.6 — New tools for spotting stacked-mark clashes. A Two marks tab in the Quality-check pairs any mark you pick (e.g. dagesh) with every other mark on every letter and flags where they overlap — handy for Babylonian pointing (vowels, dagesh & raphe all sit above) and two-vowel letters like יְרוּשָׁלִַם; the Stacked tab now also flags a vowel that collides with its trop. While placing nikkud you can preview a 2nd mark on the current letter and get a live overlap warning. Raphe now appears in the above-letter picker. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v1_7: v1.7 — Drawing aids for consistency. New guides: drop adjustable horizontal & vertical lines on the canvas — drag them or type an exact position — that stay put across every letter, perfect for matching stroke thicknesses & heights. Copy outline from another letter seeds the current letter from one you've already drawn (copy Tav, delete the toe → Het, He, Resh), then reshape with ✎ Edit points. And the built-in ḥataf-patach & ḥataf-kamatz now have their sh'va dots aligned. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v1_8: v1.8 — Kerning is easier to dial in. The big sample preview now updates live as you drag a pair's gap or add/remove pairs — not just the little two-glyph preview — so you see the effect in real words. The pair list now flags anything that won't export — ⚠ untraced glyphs or pairs still at 0 — with an "N of M pairs will be exported" summary, and highlights the pair you're editing. A reading-order hint clarifies that in Hebrew the first letter sits on the right, and class sides (Finals / Descenders) now show what they cover. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v1_9: v1.9 — More kerning power. Suggest pairs now proposes an even starting gap — set by a new Auto-tightness slider — instead of seeding zeros, so one click gets you most of the way — measured optically from the real outlines (with the correct RTL facing edges), so overhanging letters like ר & ד tuck under the next one. And you can define your own kern classes: reusable named letter groups (alongside the built-in Finals & Descenders) that you kern as a unit on either side of a pair — edit a class and every pair using it updates. (June 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_0: v2.0 — A friendlier way in. A new Take a tour walkthrough spotlights each step right on your own workspace — start it from the welcome screen, the Help header, or Getting Started. The Export button now warms the font engine in the background as soon as you trace your first letter, so your first export is quick, and it shows what it's doing while it gets ready. When something's missing, the export warnings became clickable — tap a letter to jump straight to it — and a live “what's next?” line under the letters always points you to the next thing to do. Finally, press ? anytime for a keyboard-shortcut cheat sheet. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_1: v2.1 — Custom glyphs are easier to size. The Width & margins controls now follow a letter through the Trace and Edit points steps — not just Align — so you can adjust a traced or duplicated glyph's spacing whenever you're working on its shape. Custom marks (which attach to a letter and have no width of their own) gained a Convert to main glyph button: turn a standalone symbol you built as a mark into a full glyph with its own adjustable width. And a hand-set width of zero is now respected instead of snapping back to the default. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_2: v2.2 — Wide letters, Yiddish forms & custom glyphs got a big reliability pass. Nikkud and trop now attach correctly to wide letterforms and digraphs in the exported font (they used to slide to the left edge), wide forms export with smooth curves instead of chunky outlines, and a digraph's width no longer double-counts your letter spacing. The Specialized / Yiddish / Ladino tiles now show a live preview built from your own letters — including the Width slider's stretch — and clicking a form whose base isn't traced yet jumps you straight to tracing it. The Quality check now covers custom glyphs and custom marks, custom glyphs can be picked in kerning and added to the spacing sample with one click, and a custom glyph at a form's code point is protected from being overwritten at export (with a clear note on the tile). Export also warns if custom glyphs are blank or the custom-glyphs toggle is off. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_3: v2.3 — Trop placement is safer and finer-grained. The Default spread slider no longer wipes out your hand-tuned Left/Right positions — letters you've adjusted keep their spots (with a note showing how many, and a Reset all side positions button when you really want a clean slate). A spread of 0 now sticks everywhere instead of quietly snapping back to the default. Every trop layout change — the spread, a mark's Left / Center / Right switch, and the new per-mark Height nudge — is now fully undoable (Ctrl/Cmd+Z). That Height row lets you raise or lower one trop mark on every letter, so two marks sharing a side (like Pashta and Telisha Qetana) no longer collide. And Check stacking now works while placing trop, too — preview a vowel in grey and get an instant overlap warning. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_4: v2.4 — Wide letterforms & digraphs: the margin bands and width line on the canvas now outline the composed form — not its base letter — so they sit at the real edges of a digraph and follow the Width slider live as you stretch. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_5: v2.5 — Stretching a wide letterform no longer runs it off the edge of the canvas — the workspace now widens to fit the whole composed glyph (and its right margin) at any Width, right up to 250%. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_6: v2.6 — The Place Nikkud step for a wide letterform now makes sense: it previews the vowel right on the stretched form (where it will actually sit) and gives you a one-click “Edit nikkud on …” jump to the base letter, since a wide form's vowels follow the base — no more empty screen or a “drag the handle” hint with nothing to drag. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_7: v2.7 — The mark size sliders are now undoable (Ctrl/Cmd+Z). Resizing the Nikkud, Holam, Dagesh, Holam (vav), or Trop marks and changing your mind now puts them right back — one undo step per slider drag, just like every other placement change. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_8: v2.8 — The Place Nikkud / Trop step is tidier and works the way you'd expect. A letter's placement controls — the size sliders and the ✓ Confirm placement / Reset buttons — are now grouped right below the canvas (which fills the width), so nothing's stranded in a far-off strip. The above-mark picker now only offers marks that fit the letter (the shin/sin dots show up only on Shin), and picking any mark — Holam, Shin dot, Sin dot, or Rafe — now actually previews it on the canvas (Rafe used to do nothing). (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v2_9: v2.9 — The Place Nikkud / Trop panel now says what each control affects. Sections are grouped by scope — “Qamats — every letter” for a vowel's Height & shape, “Below position — Alef only” for this letter's X / Y — with a short plain-language line under each, replacing one long confusing paragraph. The size sliders under the canvas now sit side-by-side with dividers, so they take one tidy row instead of a stack. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_0: v3.0 — Placement panel, take two: the size sliders under the canvas are stacked again (one per line, so each is easy to read), and the ✓ Confirm placement / Reset letter / Reset all buttons now sit together in their own panel to the right of the sliders instead of underneath them. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_1: v3.1 — Four fixes. The shin/sin dots are now edited in just one place — Special & precomposed forms (שׁ/שׂ) — instead of also appearing in the above-mark row. Tracing no longer clips your letter at an invisible box: it follows your whole reference image, so a wide letter's edges and feet come through. Reopening a saved project now shows honest letter status — untraced letters no longer look finished — and your chosen reference (tracing) font is kept when you reload. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_2: v3.2 — Undo now covers two more actions: showing/hiding guides and ✓ Confirm placement. Ctrl+Z steps back through both, just like every other edit. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_3: v3.3 — Small correctness fix: nikkud and trop previews now center properly on a letter whose width is set to exactly zero (a rare edge case that previously fell back to the default width). (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_4: v3.4 — "Apply outline to all letters" now asks before overwriting each letter's own outline and line-weight settings, matching the other apply-to-all buttons. (Still undoable.) (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_5: v3.5 — Autosave now also captures the opacity and overlay view sliders (template, reference image, glyph) — previously a change to only those settings could be lost if the browser closed before another edit. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_6: v3.6 — Accessibility polish. Keyboard focus now shows a clear gold outline on the letter tiles, step tabs, and buttons; the Hebrew letters in the grids are tagged as Hebrew so screen readers pronounce them with a Hebrew voice; and the on/off toggle buttons (dark mode, Default/Custom, Per Symbol/Combined, upper/lowercase, and the mark editor mode) now announce their pressed state to assistive technology. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_7: v3.7 — Edit points by keyboard. In Edit-points mode you can now select points without a mouse: , and . step to the previous / next point, and i inserts a new point after the selected one — so the existing arrow-nudge and Delete shortcuts are finally reachable keyboard-only. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v3_8: v3.8 — Crop from a sheet by keyboard. When cutting a letter or mark out of a "one image, all letters" / combined sheet, you can now do it without a mouse: the arrow keys move a crop box (Shift for smaller steps), + / − resize it, Enter crops, and Esc cancels. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_0: v4.0 — Smarter tracing and a full point-editing suite. Tracing now picks a good ink threshold automatically, can even out photo lighting, and auto-detects every letter on a combined sheet for one-click review and assignment. Edit points grew into a real outline editor: delete whole contours or stray specks, snap to guides, copy/paste points between letters, flip / rotate / scale, a selection box with move & scale handles, marquee (M) and select-all, line ↔ curve segment switches, corner rounding with a live radius preview, a pen tool (P) that draws contours point by point — even on blank glyphs like digits — and a Contours panel with per-contour colors and hide-while-editing (hidden contours still export). Imported fonts round-trip faithfully: untouched glyphs keep their exact outlines, and hand edits never silently change a glyph's width. Plus a waterfall size preview on the Spacing step. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_1: v4.1 — Auto-detect fixes. The detected-letter boxes now draw reliably in every browser — they were invisible in Firefox, which showed the sheet but not the gold boxes around each letter. And the ▦ Auto-detect letters button now sits right under the sheet, next to the page navigation, where you're already looking while boxing letters. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_10: v4.10 — Cleaner UFO exports for font editors. The UFO source export no longer invents an x-height: Hebrew has no lowercase, so that guide was just a duplicate of the cap-height line and confused font editors like Glyphs and RoboFont. The field is now simply left unset, the honest answer for a caseless font. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_11: v4.11 — More robust auto-detect review boxes. On the Auto-detect letters review screen, the outlined boxes around each detected letter now use fully self-contained sizing and styling, so they render consistently across browsers — a fix aimed at cases (notably Firefox) where the scanned sheet appeared but the boxes over it did not. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_12: v4.12 — Auto-detect review boxes render reliably in Firefox. Following up on v4.11: the detected-letter outlines are now drawn as vector paths rather than rectangles, sidestepping a Firefox quirk that collapsed the rectangle outlines to zero size — so the boxes appear over the scanned sheet as intended, in every browser. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_14: v4.14 — Auto-detect review boxes now appear in Firefox. The real culprit, finally pinned down: Firefox was hiding the entire box-overlay layer (it computed the interactive overlay group as display:none, unlike other browsers), so the detected-letter outlines and labels never showed even though the scanned sheet did. Forcing the overlay to display fixes it — the boxes now render in Firefox exactly as they do everywhere else. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_15: v4.15 — Glyph-editor warnings match the rest of the app. A few notices in the custom-glyph editor — an invalid code point, a code point that's already taken, or converting a mark that has no shape yet — used a plain browser pop-up instead of the tool's own in-app dialog. They now use the same styled dialog as every other message, so the experience is consistent throughout. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_16: v4.16 — Nikkud & trop editing controls moved beside the canvas. When you edit a vowel point or cantillation mark, its controls — the Simple editor / Upload image switch, the + Dot / + Bar buttons, the dot-size slider, and the shape toggle — now sit in the left panel next to the drawing area, instead of in a strip below it. That's the same spot the letter tools already use, so editing feels consistent, and it makes use of space that used to sit empty. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_17: v4.17 — Clicking a nikkud or trop mark opens the full shape editor. Picking a vowel point or cantillation mark in its panel now opens the same Edit-shape window used on the letter-placement screen — dots & bars, its own undo, numeric size & position fields, and one-click Apply to all letters — instead of switching the whole workspace. Marks designed from an uploaded image (and combined-sheet mode) still go straight to their image tools. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_18: v4.18 — Hebrew interface & right-to-left layout. The whole Font Maker can now switch to Hebrew — use the EN / עברית toggle in the header. Every menu, button, dialog, tooltip, and help page reads in Hebrew, the layout mirrors to right-to-left, and glyph & letter names appear in Hebrew too. Your drawing canvas and coordinates stay left-to-right, so tracing is unaffected — and switching languages never touches your open project or undo history. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_2: v4.2 — A tidier Edit points panel. The point-editing controls are reorganized into clear zones: a sticky header with Done editing always in reach, a Select / Marquee / Pen mode switch, and a middle section that shows just the actions that apply to your current selection — with a Delete ▾ button that gathers point and contour deletion in one place. The Transform, Round corners, and Contours sections now look alike and remember whether you left them open. The long help paragraph became a short tip that changes with what you're doing, plus a ? button that jumps straight to the point-editing shortcuts — and the shortcuts sheet itself now covers every mouse trick too (double-click, Alt-click, segment dots, selection-box moves). Nothing about how editing works changed — every action, shortcut, and undo behaves exactly as before. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_25: v4.25 — Choose how a vowel and a trop share a letter. When a letter carries both a vowel and a cantillation mark, the trop has always stacked right on the vowel. A new font-wide control on the Place Trop step lets you instead slide the vowel aside — left or right, with an adjustable distance — while the trop stays centered on the letter, the way many printed chumashim set it. Choose separately for below-the-letter and above-the-letter marks; stacking stays the default, previews and the quality check follow your choice, and it's fully undoable. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_26: v4.26 — A zoom slider for point editing, copy-outline within reach, and smoother corner rounding. The Edit-points view now has a drag zoom slider, so you can glide from 100% to 200% for fine work instead of clicking the + button ten times. Copy outline (reuse another letter's shape, like Kaf → Kaf sofit) and Clear outline now sit on the Align step — and Clear is in the Contours list too — so you no longer have to switch to the Trace tab to reach them. And rounding corners and nudging their handles is steadier: a handle pulled onto its own point no longer flips or spikes the curve, and rounding blends into traced (curved) outlines without a kink. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_27: v4.27 — Make a proper Bold. A new Style dropdown in Font Details (Regular / Bold) exports your font as the Bold member of its family: build or import a heavier version of your font, set Style to Bold, and export — install the Regular and Bold files together and programs like Word switch between them with the B button. Use the exact same Family name in both projects so they link up. Importing a TTF that's already marked bold sets the Style for you. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_28: v4.28 — Generate Bold, automatically. The new Generate Bold button in Font Details (also offered when you import a font) thickens every traced letter's strokes to build a real Bold weight — with a live before/after preview, an adjustable strength slider (it can lighten too), an option to keep letter heights, and matching thickening for nikkud and trop. One click sets the Style to Bold so the export links with your Regular, and one Undo reverts everything. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_29: v4.29 — Fewer points, real curves. Importing a TTF/OTF font now keeps the font's actual curves instead of flattening them into hundreds of tiny straight segments — Edit points shows roughly the points the original designer drew, and exports keep genuinely smooth curves. And when an outline has too many points (a font or SVG imported by an older version, or a heavy trace), the new Reduce points panel in Edit points cleans it up: drag the strength slider for a live preview with a running point count, release to keep it, and one Undo brings everything back. Plus a fix: importing a font's nikkud and trop mark shapes no longer stops the import with an error. And the Transform panel in Edit points gains live rotate and scale sliders: drag for a live preview around the selection's center, release to keep it — one Undo reverts, and the exact angle/percent fields are still there for precise entry. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_3: v4.3 — Sturdier exports. Your exported font now gets a valid internal name and download filename no matter what you call it — unusual family names (with slashes, brackets, %, emoji, accents, or Hebrew letters, or a name that's only spaces) used to produce a font some programs would reject or a file saved with no name; now they're always cleaned to a safe name (falling back to MyHebrewFont if nothing usable is left). And the font's version number only ticks up when an export actually finishes — a failed engine download no longer bumps it on every retry. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_4: v4.4 — Your license always comes with your font. When you export a single TTF or WOFF2, the LICENSE.txt used to try to download by itself right after the font — which some browsers quietly block, leaving you with a font and no license. Now the Exported ✓ screen gives you a one-click ⬇ LICENSE.txt button (named after your font), so it can never be missed. The TTF + WOFF2 zip and UFO still bundle it inside as before. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_5: v4.5 — A heads-up when a letter can't keep its curves. Once in a while a traced outline is too tangled for the font engine to turn its curves into the exact form a font file needs, so it quietly falls back to straight edges for that one letter — which used to happen with no warning, leaving a font that looked faceted with no clue why. Now the Exported ✓ screen tells you exactly which letters came out with straight edges, so you can re-trace or simplify just those and export again for smooth curves. Every other letter is unaffected. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_6: v4.6 — Point editing gets a proper cockpit. Everything you use while pointing at the canvas now sits in a toolbar right above it: the Select / Marquee / Pen switch, Undo / Redo buttons (handy on a tablet), zoom, and three view toggles — Handles (show curve handles on every point, not just the selected ones), Guides (hide the guide lines while you look at a shape — snapping still works), and Snap. A slim status line under the canvas shows which letter you're editing, the live cursor position in font units, and how many points are selected, so the side panel is shorter and keeps just the actions for your selection. Your first time in, a one-line hint points the way (it retires itself after your first edit). Nothing about how editing works changed — every button, shortcut, and undo behaves exactly as before (the old hint line under the canvas is retired; the ? cheat sheet has every detail). (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_7: v4.7 — Two quiet export safeguards. First: if your project somehow carries a word spacing of zero (possible in very old or hand-edited save files — the slider itself never goes below 80), the exported font used to get a zero-width space, so every word ran together; the space now always exports at least the slider's minimum width. Second: when vowels or trop are enabled, every export runs a quick shaping check to confirm the marks actually position correctly — but if that checker couldn't load (say, a flaky connection), the font downloaded anyway with only a briefly-flashed note. Now the Exported ✓ screen tells you plainly when the check was skipped, so you know to test the font before sharing it. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_8: v4.8 — Older projects export safely again. A project saved by a much older version (or edited outside the app) could be missing some of its vowel anchor points under the hood — and exporting it would fail with a generic "Export error" before your font ever built. The app now quietly restores any missing anchor points (in the same spots a fresh letter would get them) wherever it finds them — opening the anchor editor, previewing, or exporting — so those projects build normally; you can still fine-tune every anchor afterwards. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v4_9: v4.9 — Your font's version number behaves itself. Two small bookkeeping fixes: a pre-1.0 version you typed yourself (like 0.5) no longer silently becomes 1.0-something in the exported file, and the automatic per-export version tick now only sticks when a font file actually downloads — cancelling after a failed shaping check, or a WOFF2 conversion hiccup, no longer inches the version up on every retry. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_0: v5.0 — Initial release. The Hebrew Font Maker is out of beta — this is its first full public release. Thank you to everyone who tested the beta versions and shared feedback along the way. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_1: v5.1 — Dotted shin and sin now stack correctly with a holam. When a dotted shin or sin also carries a holam, the vowel dot now lands where it should — to the left of the shin-dot (two dots) or merged onto the sin-dot (one dot) — in the live preview, the QA sheet, and the exported font. You can fine-tune where the holam sits in Special & precomposed forms. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_10: v5.10 — A friendlier welcome on a tablet. If you opened the Font Maker on a tablet held upright, it used to greet you with “Best on a computer” and a ← Go back button — which was exactly backwards, because a tablet with a stylus is the device Draw mode was built for. (Tablets held sideways were already let through; upright ones are just narrow enough to trip the old check.) Now a tablet gets its own greeting that leads with drawing, plus a Start drawing button that opens the new-font setup with Drawing mode already chosen. Phones still see the original note — the fine tracing controls really are cramped on a phone. And in the guided tour, the Trace step no longer talks about turning “your picture” into an outline when you are drawing rather than uploading — it says “your drawing”, matching what you are actually looking at. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_11: v5.11 — The guided tour is one click away again, and the step buttons moved under the canvas. The walk-through was only reachable from inside the Help window, so unless you happened to open Help and spot it, there was no way back to it once you had a project on the go. There is now a ❓ Tour button in the toolbar, next to ❓ Help — the same place every other tool on the site keeps it. The step buttons moved, too: “Apply alignment to other letters…”, “Next: Trace →” and “Next: Nikkud →” used to sit far off to the right, underneath the side panels — which on most screens put them below the bottom of the window, so you had to scroll past everything to find the button that moves you along. They now sit centred directly beneath the letter you are working on, where you are already looking. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_12: v5.12 — Click a point, see its contour. In Edit points, selecting a point now draws a dashed box around the whole contour it belongs to — in the same colour as that contour’s swatch in the Contours list, where the matching row is outlined in that colour too. When a letter is a pile of overlapping contours, “which contour did I just grab?” used to mean squinting at the tint colours or hiding contours one by one; now the box on the canvas and the row in the list point at each other. Select points across several contours and each gets its own box. Like the contour colours themselves, the boxes are an editing aid only — they never appear in previews or the exported font. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_13: v5.13 — Watch a letter being written. In Draw, a new ▶ Replay button plays your strokes back one at a time, in the order you actually drew them — so you can show a class the stroke order, or check your own before you trace. It is a viewing aid and nothing more: it changes no part of the letter, adds nothing to Undo, and stops the moment you touch the canvas again. Press it a second time to stop it early. If your device is set to reduce motion, the strokes simply appear together and the Font Maker says so. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_14: v5.14 — Imported fonts keep their exact nikkud positions. Importing a TTF/OTF with anchors on now also reads each mark's own attachment point, so vowels, dagesh and trop land exactly where the original font put them — even in fonts that position, say, the sh'va and the holam through separate rules. Right after the import, every letter+mark pair is measured against the original with the same shaping engine word processors use: a status line reports the numbers, and combos that are off get a detail list with a one-click fix for the combined forms (וֹ, שׁ). Traced, drawn and built-in marks are untouched. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_15: v5.15 — Edit a partner's font from a link. Open Siddur Project starting fonts now open straight into the Font Maker from an ?start= link: a short three-step onboarding imports the font's Hebrew letters, nikkud, trop, and mark positions into a fresh project of your own, with a live preview and full credit to the original. Your version automatically keeps the original's open license — the License box locks, reserved font names ask you for a name of your own, and every export's LICENSE.txt carries the original copyright plus your "modified work" line. A new Partner fonts help tab explains the why. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_16: v5.16 — The fidelity report's Auto-fix now fixes everything it measures. After importing a font with anchors, one click corrects every flagged letter+mark combo — not just the combined forms: shared anchors move when a whole letter agrees, and the stubborn per-letter positions get exact per-letter pins, marked with the gold ✎ in the placement step. The report then re-measures against the original font and shows the after numbers, and a Fidelity report button in the Nikkud step reopens it any time. Pins stay yours: drag a pinned mark to fine-tune it, or Unpin / Clear pins to fall back to the shared anchor. Importing a font now says what it is doing: the first import of a session has to fetch the font engine, which can take a while on school Wi-Fi — and an Open Siddur edit link used to spend that whole wait sitting on an empty workspace, looking broken. A progress window now names each step and closes the moment your letters appear. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_17: v5.17 — Partner font links land with their nikkud already in place. Opening an Open Siddur ?start= edit link used to finish by handing you a fidelity report and an Apply per-combo fixes button to press before the vowels sat right. That check is now part of the loading: the progress window says “Checking where the nikkud and trop land in the original font…”, every fix it can express is applied for you, and the font is re-measured against the original before the workspace appears. The report only opens if something still missed — and it is still one click away from the Fidelity report button in the Nikkud step, with every fix undoable as a single step. Importing a font you picked yourself is unchanged: you still get the report and decide. And the tour now matches the font you actually have. A partner font arrives finished — letters drawn, vowels placed — so the from-scratch walkthrough was telling new arrivals to photograph and trace letters they already had. Partner projects now get their own seven-step tour: what came across, how to reshape a letter with Edit points, where the vowel positions came from, and which parts of Font Details are locked to the original's license and why. It is offered (pre-ticked) at the end of the partner setup, and the header Tour button gives the same one any time. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_18: v5.18 — Imported fonts now bring their English letters with them. Until now, importing a font took its Hebrew letters, vowels and cantillation marks — but quietly left every A–Z and a–z behind, so an exported font showed nothing when you typed in English. Now the import fills the English tab from the original's own Latin letters, turning the tab on for you when the font has a full alphabet, and it takes ready-made accented letters (á, é, ñ, ç) whole when the original has them — falling back to building them from your letters plus accent marks when it doesn't. If you had already drawn English letters yourself, the import asks before touching them. And English letters finally survive saving. Reopening a project used to wipe every English letter you had traced, silently, and hand it back blank — that's fixed. Punctuation, digits and symbols come across too. The font's own digits and punctuation already imported — but they shipped even when you had never traced them, so typing 5 in an exported font produced nothing at all instead of falling back to another font. An untraced one is now simply left out, and 21 more symbols (@ # $ % & * + / < = > [ ] { } | \ ^ _ ` ~) join the Punctuation & More tab — so an imported font now covers everything on a keyboard. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_19: v5.19 — An import now brings the whole font across, not just the letters. Importing a font used to stop at the alphabet: everything else a real page needs — the curly quote marks a word processor inserts for you, the en and em dashes, the ellipsis, the shekel and euro signs, © ° « » × ÷ ½ — was read and thrown away, so an exported font still fell back to another face mid-sentence. Now it all comes too, along with the standalone Latin letters (Æ Ø ß Œ Š Ž) that have no accent to build from. Your combined letters come from the original. When the source font already draws שׁ, בּ, אַ or וֹ itself, the import takes that glyph whole instead of rebuilding it from your letter plus a dot — so the dot sits exactly where the original put it (the dotted-shin pair שּׁ/שּׂ comes whole too, and the no-break space your word processor types is covered). A Rebuild from my letters button gives you the composed version back whenever you want it. The masoretic marks and the rest of the presentation forms. The masora circle and the upper and lower puncta join the Trop tab, the inverted nun and the Hebrew plus sign join Punctuation, and Specialized letters gains every remaining dagesh and mapiq form. And the line spacing matches. An import now carries the original's line metrics across, so text set in your font lines up the way the original did. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_2: v5.2 — Reach your saved fonts anytime. The My IvritSuite Fonts window — where the fonts you've saved for every IvritSuite tool live, and where you can save the one you're working on — used to appear only right after an export. It now has its own entry in the Save Project ▾ menu, so it's one click away whenever you need it. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_20: v5.20 — Rulers along the edges of the canvas. The editing canvas showed you a letter and its guide lines, but nothing about where anything sat — so matching a stroke width across two letters, or checking that a vowel cleared the baseline by the amount you meant, came down to reading numbers out of the side panels and guessing. Now numbered rulers run along the top and left edges, measured in the same font units the rest of the app uses: zero sits at the letter's origin and on the baseline, and the numbers re-space themselves as you zoom so they never crowd together. A marker on each ruler tracks your pointer, so you can always see exactly where you are. Guides you can pull off a ruler. Drag from either ruler onto the canvas and you get a guide — the same guides as before, so it is instantly draggable, renameable, and remembered with your project. And a corner that resets the zoom. The little box where the two rulers meet shows the current zoom; click it to snap straight back to 100%. Rulers start switched on — turn them off under Settings → Canvas, or press Shift + R at any time. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_21: v5.21 — Control handles stay the same size as you zoom in. Zooming in is how you do the fussy work — nudging a point onto a curve, lining a vowel up under a letter. But every dot, square and circle on the canvas used to grow along with the letter, so by 400% the handles were fat blobs sitting on top of the very outline you were trying to see, and neighbouring points ran into each other. Now they hold their size on screen no matter how far you zoom, the way they do in professional font and drawing programs: the letter gets bigger, the handles stay put, and there is far more room between them to work. Zoomed out past 50% they gently grow instead, so they never shrink away to nothing. Nothing to switch on — it just behaves this way now. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_22: v5.22 — Graph paper for the canvas. The rulers told you where you were, but nothing told you how far it was from here to there. So the everyday questions — is this stem the same width as the one on the letter before it, did this vowel land the same distance under the baseline as the last one, are these two strokes actually parallel — came down to squinting, or to dropping a guide on the canvas and deleting it again afterwards. Now you can switch on a grid across the editing canvas, measured in the same font units as everything else: zero sits on the letter's origin and on the baseline, so a line always falls exactly there. You decide how it looks and behaves. Set the spacing, how often a heavier line comes along to help you count, and how strongly the whole thing shows through — all in the new Grid panel beside the canvas, so you can watch it change as you adjust it. Zoom far out and the finest lines quietly step aside rather than smearing into a grey block. And your points can stick to it. Switch on Snap to grid and dragged points, curve handles, whole selections, pen clicks, nikkud anchors and the margin dots all settle onto the nearest grid line, exactly the way points already settle onto guides — hold Alt to slip past it for one move. The grid is a drawing aid only; it never becomes part of your font, and it is remembered on this device rather than saved into the project. It starts switched off — turn it on from the node toolbar, under Settings → Canvas, or with Shift + G at any time. Advanced Settings is now just Settings. Same tab in the same place, shorter name, with a gear on it. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_23: v5.23 — The grid now follows you in and out. The grid held one fixed spacing at every zoom, which meant it was only ever right at one zoom level: zoom out and the lines crowded together until they vanished, zoom in and they drifted so far apart there was nothing to measure against just when you were doing the finest work. Now it re-spaces itself the way the ruler numbers do. Zoom in and it fills in finer lines between the ones you set; zoom out and it steps back to coarser ones instead of disappearing. At ordinary zooms it shows exactly the Spacing you typed, and the heavier every-Nth line holds the rhythm you chose until you zoom out far enough that even that would crowd, when it steps up along with everything else. Either way the grid always agrees with the number you typed — the extra lines only ever divide it evenly or multiply it whole, never landing on some fraction in between. And you snap to what you can see. The lines it fills in are real targets, so at high zoom you can place a point on a finer division without retyping the spacing. When the grid is showing something other than your typed number, it says so right next to the field, so you always know what a drag will land on. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_24: v5.24 — Yiddish gets its pasekh tsvey yudn (ײַ). The Yiddish tab covered the two-yud digraph but not the one Yiddish actually writes most: ײַ, the standard spelling of the ay sound. Old Yiddish text stores it as a single character, and a font built here had nothing at that slot, so those words came out as empty boxes. Now the form is built from your own letters and ships with the tab — and typing the two-yud digraph followed by a pasekh composes to the very same glyph, so both spellings look identical. It also picks up your own pasekh. If you drew your own pasekh shape, it used to be quietly swapped for the standard one here; it now carries through, exactly as your own dagesh already does on שּׁ. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_25: v5.25 — Fullscreen finally means "just the canvas" while you draw. Fullscreen already hid the header and footer, but the drawing canvas still shared the screen with every settings panel — on a tablet it stayed capped at a small box with the pen tools somewhere below the fold, so a stylus meant scrolling between a stroke and its Save. Now, whenever you are actually on the Draw step in fullscreen, the settings column folds away and the canvas takes the screen — and on a wide screen the pen tools move to sit right beside it. On a tablet, where the screen is too short for that, the two Save buttons instead stay pinned to the bottom edge while you draw, so finishing a letter never means scrolling off to look for them. And if you need a pen width or a guide mid-letter, a Show Panels button in the corner brings the settings back without leaving fullscreen — the Font Maker remembers which way you like it. Leave fullscreen, or move to another step, and your normal workspace comes straight back exactly as it was. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_26: v5.26 — Tidy up a drawn letter without losing your hand. Drawing with a finger or a stylus leaves strokes that are nearly straight but not quite, and stems that stop a hair above the baseline instead of sitting on it. A new Tidy strokes button in the Draw panel fixes those two things and nothing else: a stroke that is already almost a straight line becomes one, and a loose end resting just beside a guide or the baseline moves onto it. It runs only when you press it — nothing shifts under your pen while you are drawing — and the whole tidy is a single undo, so if it smoothed away something you meant to keep, one Ctrl+Z gives your handwriting back exactly as it was. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_27: v5.27 — The graph paper is already out when you sit down. The canvas grid did everything it promised — but only for people who already knew it was there. It started hidden, so the everyday measuring questions it was built for (is this stem the same width as the last one, did this vowel clear the baseline by the amount I meant) went on being answered by eye unless you went hunting for a checkbox. It now starts switched on: open a letter and the graph paper is waiting, measured in font units from the origin and the baseline. And nothing sticks to it. A grid you did not ask for should not quietly move your work, so Snap to grid now starts off — the lines are there to measure against, and your points land exactly where you put them until you switch snapping on yourself. Both toggles are where they always were: the Grid panel beside the canvas, Settings → Canvas, or Shift + G for the grid at any time — and whichever way you set them is remembered on this device. If you had already chosen for yourself, your choice is kept. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_28: v5.28 — Type your sample text without a Hebrew keyboard. The Sample text box in the Spacing tab is where you check how your letters sit together — but it quietly assumed you could type Hebrew in the first place. Without a Hebrew layout installed you were stuck with whatever was already in the box, and even with one, nikkud and trop are close to untypeable. A new Show Hebrew Keyboard button under the field opens a full on-screen keyboard: every letter (in alef-bet order or the Israeli layout, whichever you prefer), all thirteen vowels plus the dots, and the complete set of cantillation marks. Keys type into the box at your cursor, so you can drop a vowel onto a letter you already typed, and Backspace peels off one mark at a time — exactly what you want when you are testing how a holam sits above a shin. And if your font is not set up for nikkud or trop, the matching tab says so, instead of leaving you wondering why nothing shows up in the preview. And a row of ready-made samples sits beside it. Shalom, a pangram that uses every letter, the whole alef-bet with its final forms, every vowel in turn, a cantillated verse, and Hebrew next to digits and Latin — one click each, so checking your font against the hard cases stops being a typing exercise. The same row is on the font gallery’s preview, for trying a font before you download it. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_29: v5.29 — Letters from an imported font are no longer cut off at the top or the bottom. Plenty of Hebrew fonts draw the lamed right up into the ascender, taller than the editing canvas was ever built to show — Shlomo SemiStam's climbs well past it. Import one of those and the top of the letter was simply gone: clipped off the edge of the workspace, with no zoom level and no amount of scrolling that would bring it back, and no way to grab the points up there and edit them. The canvas now grows in whichever direction it needs to — a letter that reaches into the ascender, one whose tail drops below where the canvas used to stop, or a descender line you set lower yourself — so the whole letter stays visible and editable, and the graph paper, the guides and the rulers all follow it. Letters that already fitted look exactly as they did. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_3: v5.3 — Dotted shin & sin, done right everywhere. Check stacking now shows and measures שׁ/שׂ exactly as the exported font composes them: the dot appears at its true Special-forms position and size, the vowel you're placing is measured at the form's holam slot (shown in blue), and stale or impossible pairings no longer draw or warn — so no more false 'overlaps' alarms nudging you to shrink dots that were fine. The QA sheet follows suit: dot columns on ש measure at the form's anchors, and the Two-marks tab no longer offers pairings that can't exist. The dotted forms are easier to find, too: שׁ, שׂ, וֹ, וּ, בּ and friends now sit as tiles right in the vowel picker, replacing the redundant generic tile, one click from their editor. New chips under the Spacing sample insert hard-to-type test combos — שֹׁ, שֹׂ, וֹ, וּ — and a typed וֹ previews with its own Holam (vav) size and position. Also fixed: a failed shaping-check download no longer silently stays off for the whole session — it retries on your next export. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_30: v5.30 — Imported fonts keep their kerning, their exact spacing, and their dagesh. Importing a font — the Open Siddur starting fonts included — now brings its kerning along: the pair-spacing rules modern fonts keep in their GPOS table, the ones browsers and word processors actually apply, land in the Kerning panel with every Hebrew pair intact, editable like pairs you made yourself. Word spacing now matches the original font's own space width instead of a one-size default. The dagesh finally sits where the original puts it on every letter: most Hebrew fonts record the dagesh position only inside their ready-made combined letters (בּ כּ תּ), so letters outside that set used to get a best-guess spot that left the dot floating near the top of the letter — the position is now read out of those combined letterforms themselves, and the typed form in the Spacing preview shows the original's own combined glyph, at its own width, just like the exported font. And imported vowels can no longer come in bigger than the original drew them: the mark size sliders reset to true size when a font's own marks arrive, instead of silently re-scaling the new shapes by a factor tuned for the old ones. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_31: v5.31 — An eraser that takes off only the ink you touch. The eraser in Draw mode could remove a whole stroke, or cut a stroke clean in two — but it could never shave a sliver off one side, because a stroke has one thickness all the way along and a cut always went through all of it. The eraser now has a Sculpt mode that rubs away just the ink under it: round off a corner, thin a stem, take a bite out of an edge — and the rest of the stroke stays exactly as you drew it. It is what the eraser does by default now; Partial (cut one stroke into two you can move separately) and Whole stroke are still there under Eraser mode, and each one now says in a line what it does. What you rub away is a hole in the paper rather than a change to the stroke — so if you later Move that stroke out from under it, the stroke comes back whole. Press Save drawing & trace as usual and the sculpted shape is what lands in your outline, and in the font you export. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_32: v5.32 — Choose exactly what a font import brings along. Importing a font — a TTF you upload or an Open Siddur starting-font link — used to be close to all-or-nothing: one switch for the letters, one for every vowel and cantillation shape together, one for all their positions, and the kerning came along on its own. If you wanted the original's letters but planned to place the vowels yourself, there was no way to say so. The import options now name each part separately: the letter shapes; the nikkud shapes and, on their own switch, their placement; the trop shapes and their placement; and the kerning & spacing (letter-pair kerning, word gap and line spacing). Everything starts switched on, so a plain import behaves exactly as before — un-tick the parts you mean to redo yourself and only the rest comes across. The partner wizard's What to include step offers the same choices, and what you keep stays yours: a part you left un-ticked keeps the positions you dragged and the fine-tuned pins the import would otherwise replace, and the after-import placement check only measures the parts you actually took. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_33: v5.33 — Wide letterforms for every letter. Torah scrolls and fine Hebrew typesetting stretch certain letters to fill out a line — but until now the Font Maker offered only the eight wide forms Unicode encodes, in the Specialized letters tab. A new Settings toggle, Add wide letterforms, adds a tab with a wide variant of every letter, auto-stretched from your traced letters — 150% to start, each with its own Width slider. If a stretch turns out wonky, convert that form to a fully editable glyph and fix its outline point by point (you can revert to the automatic version any time). Exported fonts include the wide letters at their code points and in a new “Wide letterforms” stylistic set (ss02), so apps that support stylistic sets can swap normal letters for wide ones with one switch. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_34: v5.34 — Many more starting fonts to edit. The partner starting-font library grew from 2 fonts to 132, drawn from the Open Siddur Project's Hebrew font collection. The bigger change is which fonts qualify: a font now counts as a starting font whenever its license lets you edit it — which is nearly all of them. Previously anything under a plain GPL was turned away, which was the wrong test: the “font exception” those licenses sometimes add only governs documents that embed a font, and has nothing to do with editing one. That reopened the whole Culmus family — David, Miriam, Frank Ruehl, Drugulin, Ellinia, Yehuda and the decorative faces — plus fonts under the Ubuntu Font Licence and Creative Commons. Your exported LICENSE.txt now spells out what the original license asks of your version: that it stays under the same license, that you note you changed it and when, that you offer your source if the license requires it, and who to credit. Where a license requires a derivative to be renamed, the Font Maker holds you to it the same way it already guards Reserved Font Names. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_35: v5.35 — Meteg, finally on the vowel line. Meteg is now a nikkud mark, not a cantillation mark: it sits beside its vowel (to the left, as Unicode expects), the pair is centered under the letter for every vowel width from hiriq to hataf, and the gap between them is read from the spacing inside your own hataf patach — or set it yourself with the new Gap slider. Works without cantillation, so siddur fonts get it too. Older projects that drew a meteg as a trop keep their shape. The Hebrew changelog also regained the missing v5.33 entry. (September 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_36: v5.36 — Right-side and mid-hataf meteg. The two Unicode spellings that move a meteg somewhere other than the left of its vowel now work: meteg + CGJ + vowel puts the meteg on the right, and hataf + ZWJ + meteg tucks the meteg between the hataf's vowel and its sheva dots — spaced by the same gap as the side-by-side pair. Nothing to set up; type the sequence and the font does the rest. (September 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_37: v5.37 — Jump straight to the next unfinished letter. A new button under the letter grid — and Shift+] / Shift+[ from anywhere in the workspace — hops to the next letter still missing its outline, or, once you are placing nikkud, still missing its anchors. It follows the same list the Next up hint and the export warnings already use, so you can work through what is left without hunting the grid for the gaps. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_4: v5.4 — Two holams, two homes. The dot of a vowel vav (וֹ, as in שָׁלוֹם) and the small dot of a consonantal vav (וֺ, as in מִצְוֺת written haser) are different characters — and now each has its own editor. The new Holam Haser tile on the vav's Above step places and reshapes the mitzvot-style dot, while the וֹ tile keeps styling the combined vowel form, with a note in each explaining which typed keys reach which. A new וֺ chip joins the Spacing test combos so you can see both side by side, and every export now verifies that a typed vav + holam really composes into your וֹ form. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_5: v5.5 — Your dagesh customizations, really in the exported font. A deep export audit found three quiet bugs in one chain: the OpenType rules that compose dotted letters (בּ, וֹ, וּ and friends) were accidentally inheriting a filter meant only for שׁ/שׂ, so in modern apps they never fired; a shin's own custom dagesh had no composed שּׁ/שּׂ form at all; and the pre-download shaping check couldn't load its engine, so it silently skipped instead of catching any of this. All three are fixed: exports now build the real שּׁ/שּׂ characters (U+FB2C/U+FB2D) from your dotted shin plus your own dagesh, every dagesh combination composes even with a vowel between the letter and the dot in the typed text, a new שּׁ chip joins the Spacing test combos, and the shaping check now genuinely runs — verifying שּׁ, בּ and בָּ before your font downloads. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_6: v5.6 — Your font, one click from a worksheet. Saving a font to My IvritSuite Fonts used to be the end of the road: the window told you to "pick them in any IvritSuite tool's font selector", but nothing took you there. Each saved font now has a "Use in Worksheet Generator" link that opens the generator with that font already chosen, so you can see your letters on a real worksheet straight away. (July 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_7: v5.7 — A guided start — and now draw your letters right on screen. Starting a font opens a three-step setup: name your font and pick a license, choose Regular or Bold plus nikkud, trope and extra alphabets, then say how your letters will arrive — and the toolbar's New no longer wipes your current project until you actually create the new one (if you left a project mid-trace, the continue prompt still appears before anything else). The biggest arrival is a brand-new Draw mode: pick Draw letters on screen and sketch each letter directly over the gray reference with a pen, finger, or mouse — pressure-sensitive stylus strokes, smoothing, a whole-stroke eraser, and a Save letter & next button that runs the tracer and moves on, so a student can flow through all 27 letters with a stylus and one button. Drawings stay editable forever, drawn and photographed letters mix freely in one font, and everything downstream — points editing, nikkud, Bold, export — works unchanged. A Show me around after setup checkbox starts the tour the moment you land in your fresh editor. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_8: v5.8 — A full pencil case for Draw mode. The on-screen drawing step now has four tools instead of two. The eraser learned to erase for real: Partial mode rubs out just the ink under your eraser — splitting a stroke into pieces when you cut through it — while Whole stroke keeps the old one-touch removal, and the eraser finally has its own size. A new Line tool lays down perfectly straight strokes (hold Shift to snap to 0° / 45° / 90°), and a new Chisel pen style turns any stroke into broad-nib calligraphy — thick horizontals, thin verticals, with an adjustable nib angle — the way a sofer's pen writes. The Move tool drags a stroke (or a lasso-selected group) anywhere, with arrow-key nudging and Delete. A cursor ring previews your exact brush or eraser footprint, one-key shortcuts switch tools (D / E / L / V, X to swap, [ and ] to resize), and an Undo button sits right in the panel for tablet drawing. The pen itself grew a full brush kit: a visual pen-style picker with five live-preview tiles — Round, Chisel, Brush (strokes that taper at both ends), Dotted (a dotted tracing line), and Hollow (outlined letters) — each with its own dial (nib angle with one-tap 0° / 45° / 90° presets, taper length, dot spacing, outline thickness). Mouse and finger strokes can vary thickness with drawing speed the way a pen does with pressure, a tilting stylus can set the chisel’s nib angle just by how you hold it, and a new Stamp tool places tagin crowns, dots, or serif feet — sized to your brush and drawn in your pen style — as ordinary strokes you can move, erase, or undo. And under every size slider, an Actual size preview window shows your exact pen stroke, eraser circle, or stamp at true canvas scale — live, as you drag. (August 2026)
fontmaker.changelog.v5_9: v5.9 — A finer pen for the fine details. Draw mode's brush and eraser now go down to a hairline — the size sliders start at 10 instead of 40 (and 20), and move a unit at a time, so tagin, thin calligraphy strokes, and small serifs are drawable without fighting the slider. Along the way, two things that quietly broke at small sizes were fixed: the Chisel pen's thin edge used to thin out to nothing below the old minimum — a small chisel stroke could save as a blank letter — and Dotted strokes had a minimum dot size that made their dots wider than the brush itself. Both now hold a floor that stays crisp when your letter is traced. The [ and ] keys also resize in smaller jumps once the brush is small. Separately, Letter Metrics moved to the right-hand column, next to Guides — it belongs to the letter rather than to any one step, so it now sits in the same place on every screen instead of at the bottom of whichever tool panel you happened to be in. And you no longer have to remember to save a drawing before moving on: opening the Trace step now traces your drawing for you, the same way it already did for scanned letters. (A letter whose points you edited by hand is left alone and asks first, since re-tracing would replace those edits — and in that case the drawing is shown greyed on the canvas with a one-click button to re-trace.) The Save buttons now sit centred under the canvas instead of at the far bottom-right. And the eraser takes out what the cursor ring covers, no more: it used to remove half a stroke-width extra at each end, so a small eraser could bite three times its own size out of a thick stroke and take a whole segment when you meant to nick a detail — it also no longer cuts a stroke it only grazed. (August 2026)
