fontmaker.help.body_anchor: Anchoring — where the vowels go. "Anchoring" means showing the font where the vowel dots (nikkud) sit on each letter — and, if you want them, the cantillation marks (trop). Turn it on first: in the Nikkud (vowels) box on the left, tick Make my font Nikkud-compatible (and the same for Trop if you'd like). The 3 · Nikkud and 4 · Trop tabs then appear. Place the anchor: a handle appears on the letter — drag it to where the mark should sit. Choose which spot you're setting: Below — for most vowels, which sit under the letter. Above (Holam) — for the dot that sits on top. Dagesh (Center) — for the dot inside the letter. Tap the vowel buttons to preview different vowels in place, and use Nikkud size to scale all the marks up or down. Your moves apply live and travel with you to the next letter — when one looks right, click ✓ Confirm placement to mark it reviewed (its dot turns a solid green ✓). Confirming is optional; undo always works. Reset letter or Reset all let you start over. A meteg sits beside its vowel, not under it: the Font Maker centers the vowel + meteg pair under the letter and spaces them by the gap it measures inside your hataf patach (change it with the Gap slider, or press Auto to go back to the measured value). 💡 For tiny adjustments, drag the handle and use your arrow keys (hold Shift for extra-fine moves), or type exact X / Y values on the right. Do this for every letter so vowels line up neatly when people type.
fontmaker.help.body_export: Exporting & installing your font. When your letters are ready, choose a format in the picker next to ⬇ Export TTF (top-right), then click the button. It builds a real font from your work. Which format? TTF (recommended) — a normal font file to install and type with in Word, Google Docs, Canva — anywhere you choose fonts. Start here. WOFF2 (web) — a compressed font for embedding on a website. TTF + WOFF2 (zip) — both files plus a ready-to-paste @font-face CSS snippet. UFO source (zip) — an editable source for font editors (FontForge, Glyphs, RoboFont), with real curves, anchors and a features.fea. Every export comes with a LICENSE.txt — the license you picked in Font Details, with your name as author. The TTF + WOFF2 zip and the UFO keep it inside the download; a single TTF or WOFF2 offers it as a one-click ⬇ LICENSE.txt button on the Exported ✓ screen. Install the TTF: Mac: double-click the .ttf file, then click Install Font. Windows: right-click the .ttf file and choose Install. Then pick your font by name wherever you choose fonts. 💡 The very first export downloads a one-time font engine (about 8 MB), so give it a moment — after that it's quick. Check it & share it. The 🔍 QA Check button scans every letter–mark pair for collisions (see the QA Check tab), and saving your font to ★ My IvritSuite Fonts lets you read with your font right inside any IvritSuite tool (see the Use in IvritSuite tab). Preview PDF. The Preview PDF button (top bar) makes a printable specimen sheet — a cover page plus a chart of every letter paired with each vowel. A great way to proofread your whole font on one page before you install it. Made changes and re-exporting? The version number ticks up automatically each time. If you'd already installed an older copy, delete it first so your computer picks up the new one. (If some letters aren't traced or anchored yet, the tool warns you — those letters would come out blank.)
fontmaker.help.body_ivritsuite: Use this font in IvritSuite. You can read with your own font right inside any IvritSuite tool's font picker — without installing anything on your computer. Save it: export your font (any format), then on the Exported ✓ success screen click ★ My IvritSuite Fonts and choose ★ Save current font. Your font is stored in this browser. Manage them: the My IvritSuite Fonts window lists everything you've saved, each with buttons to download or remove it. Keep up to 10 — saving an 11th drops the oldest. Use it: open any IvritSuite tool (e.g. Torah Trainer) in this same browser, open its font picker, and pick your font under My Fonts. Your letters, vowels and trop all render using the anchors you set here. ⚠️ Saved fonts live on this browser, on this device — this isn't a cloud account. To use a font on another computer, export the TTF and save it there too. Clearing your browser data removes saved fonts.
fontmaker.help.body_licenses: Choosing a license. Your license tells the world what others may do with your font. Pick one in the Font Details box — it's written into the font and into the LICENSE.txt that downloads with your export. They're listed from most open to most strict: Public Domain (CC0) — you give up all rights; anyone can use, change, sell, or share it freely, no credit needed. The most generous option. SIL Open Font License 1.1 (OFL) — the standard for free fonts: anyone may use, study, modify, and share it (even bundled in paid software), but it can't be sold on its own and must stay under the OFL. MIT — very permissive: do almost anything, just keep the copyright + permission notice. All Rights Reserved — fully proprietary: nobody may use, copy, or modify it without your written permission. The most restrictive. 💛 If you can, choose a more open license (CC0, OFL, or MIT). Open Hebrew fonts are a real gift for students, teachers, and anyone learning to read — they make your work usable in classrooms, siddurim, and projects you'll never even see. ⚠️ Every license generated here includes a Made with IvritSuite.com attribution line. This line must stay in the LICENSE file — it's what keeps the tool free for everyone.
fontmaker.help.body_oslock: Partner fonts — why the license is locked. Some projects start from an existing open-licensed font shared by a partner like the Open Siddur Project. Your edited font is legally a modified version of that original — and open font licenses (like the SIL Open Font License and the GPL) require modified versions to stay under the same license as the original. That's not a limitation IvritSuite adds; it's the very rule that makes the original free for you to edit in the first place. So on these projects the License box is locked to the original's license, and every export's LICENSE.txt carries the original copyright plus your "modified work" line. Why you may need a new name. Many open fonts declare Reserved Font Names — names that only the original may use. A modified version must be renamed so nobody confuses it with the original. If the original reserves names, the Family name you pick can't contain them — add your own name or your school's instead (e.g. "Kehilla SemiStam"). The Reserved name field shows the original's reserved names, read-only. What actually carries over. Your export is rebuilt by IvritSuite from the letters in the editor: the original's Hebrew letterforms, vowels, cantillation marks, mark positions, its ready-made combined forms (שׁ בּ אַ), Latin letters, punctuation, symbols, line metrics and kerning pairs come along; its hinting and hand-tuned internals don't. The LICENSE.txt records exactly what your version is based on. 💛 The "made with IvritSuite" line on these exports is informational only — the original's license terms are the ones that apply, unchanged.
fontmaker.help.body_qa: QA Check — catch collisions before you export. Click 🔍 QA Check (top bar) to open a grid showing every letter paired with every vowel and trop mark. It reads your font silently — it never changes anything. Red cells flag a real ink collision worth a look: a mark sitting on top of the letter's ink (overlapping it), or a below mark running into a letter's descender tail — the part that hangs below the line, like ך or ק. To fix one, go back to the 3 · Nikkud or 4 · Trop step for that letter and nudge its anchor (or shrink Nikkud size), then re-check. 💡 A note at the top warns when a tall mark or letter will expand the font's vertical box — that's expected and exports fine; it just means the font grew a little taller. And not every red cell is a disaster: glance at each and trust your eye.
fontmaker.help.body_saving: Saving your project. Your project is your work-in-progress — all your images, outlines, anchors and settings. Save it so you can come back and keep editing later. Save Project (top bar) gives you two choices. To computer downloads a single .hebrewfont file with everything packed inside — your permanent backup. In this browser keeps a quick copy on this device that you can reopen any time from Load Project ▾ → Recent. Load Project ▾ reopens a saved .hebrewfont file from your computer, or a recent in-browser save. ⚠️ This is your editable project, not the font itself. To get a font you can install and type with, see the Exporting & Installing tab. The browser copy (and the automatic safety-net save) is handy, but it is not a real backup — if you clear your browser data or switch computers, it's gone. Save “To computer” regularly to keep a file you can't lose.
fontmaker.help.body_share: Share your font. Made a font you're proud of? Open Hebrew fonts are a real gift to teachers, students, and siddur-makers. Here are good places to share yours. ⚠️ Wherever you share, include your LICENSE.txt (every export provides one — inside the zip/UFO, or via the ⬇ LICENSE.txt button for a single TTF/WOFF2). Most platforms below require an open license such as the SIL Open Font License (OFL) — set one in the Font Details box and re-export if needed. Google Fonts — the largest home for free fonts; once accepted, anyone can use yours on the web (OFL required). See the submission guide and onboarding docs. Open Siddur — Hebrew font pack — a curated, open-source Unicode Hebrew font collection for liturgical and educational use: opensiddur.org/help/fonts. The Open Font Library — upload and share libre fonts directly: fontlibrary.org. The Culmus Project — the long-running home of free Hebrew fonts: github.com/Culmus. Alef Alef Alef (אלף אלף אלף) — Israel's community library of free, libre Hebrew fonts; browse the collection and share your own: alefalefalef.co.il. GitHub — publish your font and its license in a public repo so others can find and improve it (also the usual first step toward Google Fonts). Add it to IvritSuite. I'd love to feature your font in the IvritSuite font library. To submit it, use the 📤 Share this font button on the export-success screen — or the ✚ Submit a font button on the Resources → Fonts page. Either one opens a pre-filled submission email to Harrison@IvritSuite.com. Fill in or confirm these details, then attach your files: Font name and type — Block / Cursive / Torah / Other. Whether it supports nikkud and trop. Its license (CC0 / OFL / MIT / Other) and version. Your name and website (optional). 📎 Attach the exported font file (TTF / OTF / WOFF) and its LICENSE.txt — the zip/UFO already include it; for a single TTF/WOFF2, grab the ⬇ LICENSE.txt button on the Exported ✓ screen. 💛 Open licenses (CC0, OFL, MIT) let your font reach classrooms, siddurim, and projects you'll never even see. If you can, share it freely.
fontmaker.help.body_spacing: Spacing. Open the Spacing panel on the left to control the gaps in your finished font. A live preview updates as you slide: Letter spacing — the gap between letters. Word spacing — the width of the space between words. Line spacing — the gap between lines of text. Kerning — fine-tune the gap for specific letter pairs that need it (some combinations look too tight or too loose at the default spacing). Pick the two sides, set the gap, and click Add pair — it's saved as real OpenType kerning and shows in the preview. Sample text — type any Hebrew here to see how it looks. Reset spacing puts everything back to the defaults. 💡 The preview uses your traced letters. Any letter you haven't traced yet shows up as a dashed box — that's just a placeholder, not part of your font.
fontmaker.help.body_start: Welcome 👋 Hebrew Font Maker turns your hand-drawn Hebrew letters into a real font you can install on your computer and type with — vowels (nikkud) and cantillation marks (trop) included. ▶ Take a tour · ⌨ Keyboard shortcuts. Here's the whole journey, start to finish: Add your letters — upload a clear picture of each one, or draw them right on screen. Trace — the tool turns each picture into a clean outline. Anchor — show where the vowel dots sit on each letter. Spacing — fine-tune the gaps between letters and words. Export & install — download your finished font and use it anywhere. Use the tabs above to read about each step. You can work through them roughly in order, one letter at a time. Before you start, give your font a name in the Font Details box (top-left). The Family name is what you'll see in font menus later. The version number takes care of itself. 💡 Works best on a desktop or laptop. Your work is auto-saved in this browser as you go, but use Save Project for a real backup you can keep (see the Saving tab). Made a mistake? Undo / Redo — the ↶ ↷ buttons in the top bar, or Ctrl/⌘-Z and Ctrl/⌘-Shift-Z — step back and forth through your edits. Press ? anytime for the full list of keyboard shortcuts.
fontmaker.help.body_templates: Printable handwriting templates. Prefer to write on paper? Print one of these worksheets, fill the boxes with your own Hebrew, then scan or photograph the page and bring it back in here to build your font. How it works: Print a template below at actual size (100% — turn "Fit to page" off), on plain white paper. Write one glyph or mark per box, in dark ink. The small blue label in each corner shows what goes there — a reference glyph, its name, and its U+ code. For vowels and trop it also says below / above / center so you know where the mark sits on the letter. Scan at 300 DPI or higher (or take a straight-on, evenly-lit photo with no shadows). Save it as a PNG or a high-quality JPG. Import it on the Uploading step: choose One image with all letters, then drag a box around each glyph to cut it out. 💡 The grid prints in light blue on purpose: the tracer only keeps dark ink, so the blue boxes and labels disappear by themselves — just keep your writing dark and inside each box. (Keep the Ink threshold near its default; pushing it much higher can start to pick up the light grid.) ✍️ A black or dark-blue felt-tip or fineliner reads far better than pencil or a light ballpoint. Write boldly and fill the box. Download a template — PDF to print, or Picture for an image file. ⚠️ The Letters and English Letters sheets are two pages each — each downloads as a 2-page PDF, or as two numbered images (…_1.png, …_2.png) when you choose Picture.
fontmaker.help.body_trace: Tracing. Tracing turns your photo into a smooth outline the font can actually use. Open the 2 · Trace tab — the first time, it traces automatically. If it doesn't look right, nudge these: Ink threshold — how dark a spot has to be to count as ink. Slide it down if light strokes are being missed, or up if the paper/background is bleeding in. Detail (less ↔ more) — slide left for a smoother, cleaner outline; right to hug every little bump of your handwriting. Invert (light ink on dark) — turn this on if you wrote in white or light ink on a dark background. Click Re-trace to redo it with your new settings, or Clear to start the letter over. The dot turns blue once a letter is traced. Fine-tune the outline by hand. Once a letter is traced, click ✎ Edit points to tidy the shape: drag any point to move it, nudge the selected point with the arrow keys (hold Shift for bigger steps), or press Delete to remove it. Click Done editing when it looks right. 💡 The holes inside letters like ס, ם and ע are found and punched out for you automatically.
fontmaker.help.body_upload: Uploading your letters. You'll add each of the 27 Hebrew letters — from a picture, from a font file, or by drawing them on screen. If you're using pictures, clear dark ink on white paper works best. Pick how you want to add them in the Add Letters panel on the left: One letter per image — upload one photo per letter. Simplest if you're scanning or photographing letters one at a time. One image with all letters — upload one photo of a whole sheet of letters, then pick a letter and drag a box around it to cut it out. Existing font file — already have a font file? Import it and the letters come in ready-made, so you can skip tracing entirely. Draw letters on screen — no scanner needed: draw each letter with a pen, finger, or mouse, right on the canvas over a faint reference letter. Allowed files: any image — PNG, JPG, GIF or WebP. Transparent PNGs and letters drawn on a plain white background also work great. (For the Existing font file option, a TTF or OTF font file.) ✒️ Have vector artwork? Turn on Enable SVG uploading under Settings → Input mode to drop in SVG files — their vector paths become the glyph outlines directly, with no tracing. See the SVG Upload Guide there for naming one sheet so its letters auto-split. Tracing guide: a faint reference letter shows behind yours so you can line things up. On the right of the canvas, dial the Reference letter opacity slider (or untick Show reference glyph behind to hide it), and use Imported image opacity to fade your own photo in or out. Position it (the 1 · Align step): click a letter in the grid on the left, then use the adjustment buttons on the left of the canvas — Wider, Taller, Rotate, Skew — to sit your letter neatly on the guide lines. The little dot on that letter turns orange once it has an image. 🖨️ Don't have letters to scan yet? The Download Templates tab gives you printable sheets — handwrite each letter in the boxes, scan or photograph the page, then bring it in here with One image with all letters.

fontmaker.modals.svg_only_msg: Only SVG files can be uploaded while SVG mode is on.
fontmaker.modals.svgguide_body: SVG only. With this mode on, every upload zone accepts only .svg files. The vector paths become your glyph outlines directly — there is no tracing step, so the shapes stay exact. One letter per file. Choose One letter per image, pick a letter, and drop its SVG. It opens straight on the Nikkud step with the outline already in place. Auto-split one big sheet. Put every letter in a single SVG and name each element so it maps to a glyph — set the element's id (or Inkscape label) to one of: uni05D0 / u05D0 / glyph05D0 (the Unicode hex), the literal Hebrew letter, e.g. א, the English name, e.g. Alef, Kaf-sofit. Then choose One image with all letters, drop the SVG, and matches assign automatically (or click Auto-split by name). Box the rest by hand. Anything unnamed can still be selected: drag a box around a letter on the sheet and the shapes inside it become that glyph. Auto-fit. Each imported outline is scaled to the cap height and seated on the baseline (descenders dip below). Use Edit points and the Width / side-bearing controls to fine-tune. New shapes / PUA. For glyphs that aren't standard characters, turn on Add custom glyphs and import the SVG at a Private-Use code point (U+E000–U+F8FF). Tips: group transforms are honored, so flatten/ungroup freely; convert strokes to fills first (open strokes don't fill); clipped, masked, hidden, and <use>-referenced elements are skipped.

fontmaker.ostour.step_1_body: Every letter came across from {font} — already drawn, already spaced, with its vowel positions. Nothing to scan or trace.
fontmaker.ostour.step_2_body: Pick a letter, open this step, then use Edit points to reshape its outline. Letters you never touch stay exactly as the original drew them.
fontmaker.ostour.step_3_body: Nikkud and trop came from {font} and were measured against it while your font loaded. Fidelity report here shows what was checked; drag a mark to adjust it.

fontmaker.ostour.step_7_body: Download a real installable font. Its LICENSE.txt carries {font}'s copyright plus your own “modified work” line — and if your font's name still contains a reserved name, export will stop and send you back to Font Details.

fontmaker.oswizard.need_name_author: Enter a font name and your name to continue.

fontmaker.panels.above_hint: The holam dot and rafe sit above the letter. Edit shape redesigns the selected mark.
fontmaker.panels.above_hint_shin: The שׁ/שׂ tiles open Special & precomposed forms — the one place the shin/sin dots are placed.
fontmaker.panels.above_hint_vav: Holam Haser is the consonantal-vav dot (מִצְוֺת), typed as vav + holam-haser. A typed vav + regular holam becomes the וֹ combined form instead.
fontmaker.panels.adv_custom_hint: Adds a Custom glyphs tab (after Punctuation) where you can define glyphs at any Unicode code point — a main letter or a nikkud mark. Tip: for brand-new shapes use the Private-Use range U+E000–U+F8FF so they don't collide with standard characters.
fontmaker.panels.adv_english_hint: Adds an English tab to design A–Z and a–z (with an uppercase/lowercase switch). Importing a font fills this tab from its own Latin letters. Accent-supporting letters can carry accents (á, é, ñ, ç…). Template: PDF · PNG
fontmaker.panels.adv_grid_hint: Graph paper across the editing canvas, spaced in font units like the rulers — handy for matching stroke widths and keeping vowels a consistent distance from the baseline. It re-spaces itself as you zoom — finer divisions on the way in, coarser ones on the way out — and snapping follows what is on screen. Spacing, the heavier every-Nth line, opacity and snapping live in the Grid panel beside the canvas, where you can see them change. Shortcut: Shift + G.
fontmaker.panels.adv_grid_title: Show graph-paper grid lines across the editing canvas (Shift + G)
fontmaker.panels.adv_ladino_hint: Adds a Ladino (Judeo-Spanish) tab: the rafe / varika letters (בֿ גֿ דֿ זֿ טֿ פֿ קֿ) plus שׁ / שׂ — composed from your traced letters.
fontmaker.panels.adv_rulers_hint: Numbered rulers along the top and left of the editing canvas, measured in font units — zero sits at the letter's origin and on the baseline. A marker on each ruler follows your pointer, and the corner box shows the zoom (click it to snap back to 100%). Drag off a ruler onto the canvas to drop a new guide. Shortcut: Shift + R.
fontmaker.panels.adv_rulers_title: Show rulers along the top and left of the editing canvas (Shift + R)
fontmaker.panels.adv_special_hint: Adds a Specialized letters tab with the wide letterforms (wide alef, dalet, he, kaf, lamed, final mem, resh, tav) and the rest of the dagesh & mapiq presentation forms (גּ דּ הּ טּ לּ מּ …) — all auto-composed from your traced letters, with a Width slider on the wide ones.
fontmaker.panels.adv_svg_hint: Upload SVG files instead of images — vector paths become the glyph outlines directly, with no tracing. In this mode the upload zones accept SVG only. SVG Upload Guide →
fontmaker.panels.adv_wide_hint: Adds a Wide letterforms tab with a wide variant of every letter — auto-stretched from your traced letters (150% to start, each with its own Width slider), and convertible to a fully editable glyph when a stretch needs hand-fixing. The exported font also gets a Wide letterforms stylistic set (ss02) that swaps normal letters for wide ones in apps that support it.
fontmaker.panels.adv_yiddish_hint: Adds a Yiddish tab: pasekh/komets alef (אַ אָ), the rafe letters (בֿ כֿ פֿ), the digraphs tsvey vovn / vov-yud / tsvey yudn (װ ױ ײ), and pasekh tsvey yudn (ײַ) — all composed from your traced letters.

fontmaker.panels.center_v_title: Center vertically — halfway between the top and base lines

fontmaker.panels.combined_drop_img: Drop your sheet(s) here, or click to browse — add more than one for multi-page templates.

fontmaker.panels.confirm_placement_title: Marks this letter's placement as reviewed. Undo (Ctrl+Z) always works — confirming isn't required to keep your changes.
fontmaker.panels.copy_outline_title: Start this letter from another letter's outline
fontmaker.panels.custom_empty: No custom glyphs yet — add one below
fontmaker.panels.custom_glyphs_hint: Define a glyph at any Unicode code point. Brand-new shapes work best in the Private-Use range U+E000–U+F8FF. Trace each glyph like a letter, or duplicate an existing letter and tweak it.
fontmaker.panels.custom_mark_hint: A mark attaches to a letter and has no width of its own. For a standalone symbol that needs its own spacing, choose Main glyph instead.
fontmaker.panels.dagesh_follows_hint: The dagesh's position follows the letter's own Dagesh (Center), so {glyph} always matches a dagesh you place on the plain letter — to move it, edit the letter's Dagesh (Center) on its Nikkud step. Its size you can set right here:
fontmaker.panels.dagesh_size_hint: Sizes the dot for this form only — the regular vowel dot on other letters stays the same.
fontmaker.panels.default_spread_hint: Default distance Left/Right marks shift from center, on all letters (per-letter tweaks come after).
fontmaker.panels.default_width_hint: Default width — drag the slider to customize.
fontmaker.panels.drag_handle_hint: Drag the handle (or arrow keys; Shift = 1 unit), or edit X/Y on the left, to position the {class} mark.
fontmaker.panels.draw_pen_title: This glyph is blank — draw its outline point by point
fontmaker.panels.draw_pen_title2: No trace yet — draw the outline point by point instead
fontmaker.panels.edit_shape_square_hint: Make the dot a square or redesign it. Applies to this form (via its base letter); choose “all letters” in the editor to change it everywhere.
fontmaker.panels.eng_accent_drag_hint: Pick an accented form on the left, then drag the orange dot to position the accent. Accents are baked into precomposed letters (á, é, ñ, ç…) when you export.
fontmaker.panels.eng_accent_note: These came ready-made from the imported font. {count} of them can be rebuilt from your own letters plus accent marks.
fontmaker.panels.eng_accent_rebuild_conf: Drop {count} ready-made accented forms and rebuild them from your own letters plus accent marks?
fontmaker.panels.eng_accents_hint: Pick an accented form, then drag the accent into place on the canvas (or type X / Y). Each is baked into the exported font.
fontmaker.panels.eng_no_accents: This letter has no accented forms — it's ready once traced.
fontmaker.panels.eng_no_accents_done: No accents for this letter — it's done once traced.
fontmaker.panels.even_lighting_aria: Even out lighting — remove photo shadows before tracing
fontmaker.panels.font_drop: Drop a font (TTF/OTF) here, or click to browse.
fontmaker.panels.form_enable_tab: Enable this tab to add its forms.
fontmaker.panels.form_need_trace: Trace these base letters to fill in this tab:
fontmaker.panels.form_src_ctl_hint: This form came ready-made from the imported font — its dot is part of the glyph, so there is nothing to place or size here.
fontmaker.panels.form_src_note: {count} of these came ready-made from the imported font.
fontmaker.panels.form_src_rebuild_confir: Drop {count} ready-made forms and rebuild them from your own letters plus marks?
fontmaker.panels.form_src_stage: This form came ready-made from the imported font — there is no mark to place.
fontmaker.panels.grid_hint: Grid lines are measured in font units from the letter's origin and the baseline, so zero always lands on a line. The spacing re-fits itself as you zoom, and snapping follows whatever is on screen. The grid is a drawing aid only — it never becomes part of your font.
fontmaker.panels.grid_major_title: Draw a heavier line every Nth grid line — 0 for none. The heavy lines keep the rhythm you set here, whatever the zoom fills in between them.
fontmaker.panels.grid_opacity_title: How strongly the grid shows through
fontmaker.panels.grid_snap_title: Snap dragged points, curve handles, nikkud anchors and margin dots to the grid lines you can see — so zooming in lets you land on a finer division (needs Snap on in the node bar; Alt bypasses)
fontmaker.panels.grid_step_title: Distance between grid lines in font units (1–1000). The grid divides this evenly as you zoom in and steps up in whole multiples as you zoom out, so it stays readable at any zoom.
fontmaker.panels.guides_empty: Add a guide, then drag it on the canvas or type an exact position (font units). Guides stay put across every letter — handy for matching stroke thicknesses & heights.
fontmaker.panels.halign_hint: Sets where {name} sits across every letter. Position tweaks belong to the column (Left / Center / Right) — and stay with it if you switch sides.
fontmaker.panels.height_trop_hint: Raises or lowers just {name} on every letter — e.g. to separate two marks sharing a side.
fontmaker.panels.height_vowel_hint: Height raises or lowers just {name} — on every letter. Edit shape redesigns its dots & bars.
fontmaker.panels.holam_vav_hint: Sizes the dot on every וֹ — the same Holam (vav) size control as the vav's Nikkud step. (The standalone holam on other letters is sized by Nikkud size.)
fontmaker.panels.holam_vav_vs_haser: This וֹ is what a typed vav + holam becomes (as in שָׁלוֹם). The consonantal vav of מִצְוֺת uses the separate Holam Haser mark — style its dot on the vav's Above step.
fontmaker.panels.kern_autotightness_hint: Negative = tighter, positive = looser (font units). “Suggest pairs” seeds an even starting gap toward Auto-tightness (lower = tighter), measured optically so overhanging letters tuck in; Preview PDF shows it shaped in full.
fontmaker.panels.kern_classes_hint: Reusable letter groups — pick one on either side of a pair. Editing a class updates every pair that uses it.
fontmaker.panels.kern_export_skip: Pairs marked “⚠ untraced” or “set a gap” are skipped.
fontmaker.panels.kern_no_pairs: No pairs yet — pick two glyphs (or a class on either side) and Add.
fontmaker.panels.kern_preview_note: Preview shows one member of each class.
fontmaker.panels.kern_reading_hint: Type the pair in reading order — in Hebrew the first letter sits on the right.
fontmaker.panels.kern_setgap_title: Pairs at 0 do nothing — drag the gap to apply.
fontmaker.panels.kern_untraced_title: A glyph in this pair has no traced outline — it will be skipped on export.
fontmaker.panels.ladino_intro: Ladino (Judeo-Spanish) forms: each base letter with the rafe / varika bar, composed from your traced letters.
fontmaker.panels.legend_align: Drag the letter to move · corner ◻ scales (keeps shape) · side ▭ squishes that direction · ● rotates.
fontmaker.panels.legend_anchors: Previewing the {name} vowel — drag the handle, or use arrow keys (Shift = 1 unit).
fontmaker.panels.legend_trace: Adjust threshold & smoothing, then Trace. Corners stay crisp; counters punch out.
fontmaker.panels.legend_wideform: Nikkud preview — the position follows the base letter (edit it there).
fontmaker.panels.letter_allowed_svg: Allowed: SVG only — vectors import directly (no tracing).
fontmaker.panels.license_hint: Pick how others may use your font. Every export's LICENSE.txt lists your name as author and includes a required Made with IvritSuite.com line. The version ticks up each export — edit it anytime.
fontmaker.panels.load_no_recent: No recent projects yet — save one first.
fontmaker.panels.lower_mark_title: Lower this mark on every letter
fontmaker.panels.lower_vowel_title: Lower this vowel on every letter
fontmaker.panels.mark_allowed_img: Allowed: any image file — PNG, JPG, GIF, WebP.
fontmaker.panels.mark_click_box: Click a mark, then drag a box around it on the sheet. Undesigned marks use the default shape.
fontmaker.panels.mark_click_design: Click a mark to design it (draw or upload). Undesigned marks use the default shape.
fontmaker.panels.mark_coming_soon: Custom {label} marks & the built-in set are coming in the next update.
fontmaker.panels.mark_drop_combined: Drop a {svg}sheet of {label} symbols, or click to browse.
fontmaker.panels.mark_pick_then_box: Then pick a symbol below and drag a box around it on the canvas.
fontmaker.panels.mark_sheet_loaded: Sheet loaded ✓ — pick a symbol below, then drag a box around it on the canvas.
fontmaker.panels.mark_shevana: Add a bold Sheva Na (so na & nach stand apart)
fontmaker.panels.mark_shevana_hint: Exports a heavier sheva alongside the normal one. To make a sheva bold in Word, select the letter and turn on Stylistic Set 1; or insert the character U+E0B0 in its place. Readers can then see which sheva is mobile (na) vs. silent (nach).
fontmaker.panels.mark_trop_hint: Trop attaches to the typed letter (and stacks above/below a vowel). In Place Trop each mark can sit Left, Center, or Right of the letter — sensible defaults are set (Segol, Zarqa, Pashta & Telisha Qetana go left; Geresh Muqdam, Deḥi, Yetiv & Telisha Gedola go right) and you can change any of them. Left / Right marks land at the leading / trailing edge of their own letter — exact at a word's edge, approximate mid-word (true word-position placement isn't done).
fontmaker.panels.markctl_box_hint: Drag a box around {name} on the sheet above to bring it into the editor. Keyboard: arrows move the box, +/− resize, Enter to crop.
fontmaker.panels.markctl_combined_hint: Combined mode: upload a sheet of {label} symbols in the sidebar first, then drag a box around {name}.
fontmaker.panels.markctl_hint: Click a piece to select; drag to move, drag the ◻ corner to resize. A bar's corner can be dragged for any width/thickness. Build the mark from dots & bars — it's seeded from the default shape.
fontmaker.panels.markctl_region_hint: Region selected for {name}. Fine-tune below, then trace.
fontmaker.panels.markctl_svg_imported: Imported from SVG ✓ — re-drop to replace.
fontmaker.panels.markstage_above: Above-vowel — draw it ABOVE the line (sits over the letter).
fontmaker.panels.markstage_center: Center mark — draw it ON the line (sits in the letter body).
fontmaker.panels.markstage_under: Under-vowel — draw it BELOW the line (sits under the letter).
fontmaker.panels.meteg_auto_title: Use the spacing inside your own hataf patach as the gap
fontmaker.panels.meteg_hint: Font-wide. A meteg sits to the left of its vowel; the pair is centered under the letter. Right-side and mid-hataf meteg follow the Unicode sequences (CGJ / ZWJ).
fontmaker.panels.metric_fit_title: Give this letter the font's default left/right margins around its current outline (undoable)
fontmaker.panels.metric_hint: Check Adjust margins manually? to show draggable dots: drag the left dot to slide the whole letter, the right dot to set the right margin, and width to set the advance. Fit margins gives a redrawn letter the font's default side margins. (The reference image stays draggable either way.)
fontmaker.panels.metric_lsb_drag: Left margin — drag to slide the whole letter
fontmaker.panels.next_title: Next letter ( ] ) — stays on this step
fontmaker.panels.nexthint_nikkud: Letters done! Place nikkud on {name} — {count} to go.
fontmaker.panels.nexthint_qa: All 27 letters ready — run QA Check, then Export.
fontmaker.panels.nexthint_start: Start by uploading and tracing your first letter.
fontmaker.panels.pair_hint: Font-wide. Stack puts the trop right on the vowel; Slide moves the vowel sideways so the trop stays centered on the letter.
fontmaker.panels.pair_slide_left_title: The vowel moves left; the trop stays centered on the letter
fontmaker.panels.pair_slide_right_title: The vowel moves right; the trop stays centered on the letter
fontmaker.panels.pair_stack_title: The trop sits directly on the vowel (default)
fontmaker.panels.pair_title: When a letter has both a vowel and a trop
fontmaker.panels.pick_then_box: Pick a letter, then drag a box around it on the sheet to bring it into the editor. Keyboard: arrows move the box, +/− resize, Enter to crop.
fontmaker.panels.pill_carried_title: These positions were carried from the previous letter. Review them, then Confirm.
fontmaker.panels.pill_unconfirmed_title: This letter's placement hasn't been confirmed yet. Adjust if needed, then Confirm — undo always works.
fontmaker.panels.precomp_drag_hint: Placing a precomposed form — drag the orange dot on the canvas, or type X / Y on the left. Your change is saved automatically.
fontmaker.panels.precomp_holam_hint: Where a holam sits when it's typed on this dotted letter. Default: opposite the shin-dot (two dots) or merged onto the sin-dot (one dot). Drag the blue dot, or type X / Y.
fontmaker.panels.precomp_where_hint: Where the mark sits in the combined glyph. Drag the orange dot on the canvas, or type X / Y. Affects this precomposed form only — saved automatically.
fontmaker.panels.prev_title: Previous letter ( [ ) — stays on this step
fontmaker.panels.punct_include: Include digits & punctuation in my font
fontmaker.panels.punct_off_hint: Currently off: these glyphs are skipped on export and have no practice page. Turn it on to include them.
fontmaker.panels.punct_on_hint: Included in the exported font & the Punctuation practice template. Trace each one like a letter — digits start blank; punctuation comes pre-shaped.
fontmaker.panels.raise_mark_title: Raise this mark on every letter
fontmaker.panels.raise_vowel_title: Raise this vowel on every letter
fontmaker.panels.reference_upload_allowe: Allowed: TTF or OTF font files.
fontmaker.panels.reset_side_positions_ti: Re-seed every letter's Left/Right columns from its center ± spread (undoable)
fontmaker.panels.shin_stack_note: In the font, שׁ/שׂ + a vowel become one combined glyph: the dot is baked in, and the vowel or mark that follows attaches at the form's holam slot — shown here in blue. Both positions live in Special & precomposed forms (below).
fontmaker.panels.side_positions_kept.one: {count} letter's hand-tuned side positions kept — the slider only moves columns still at the default.
fontmaker.panels.side_positions_kept.oth: {count} letters' hand-tuned side positions kept — the slider only moves columns still at the default.
fontmaker.panels.sin_stack_merged_note: A holam on שׂ traditionally merges with the sin dot into a single dot, so these two marks are meant to coincide. You can still move the holam in Special & precomposed forms below.
fontmaker.panels.sin_stack_separate_note: The holam sits clear of the sin dot here, so שֹׂ will show two separate dots. Drag the holam in Special & precomposed forms below if you want the traditional single merged dot.
fontmaker.panels.size_hint: Nikkud size scales the vowels and the shin/sin dot (unless a שׁ/שׂ form has its own Dot size, which wins). Holam size controls just the standalone holam dot above the letter, so you can make it thinner than the below vowels. Dagesh size controls just the dagesh dot.
fontmaker.panels.size_hint_vav: Holam (vav) size controls just the dot on the vav (וֹ), so you can grow it as part of the letter.
fontmaker.panels.spacing_hint: Adjusts the exported font's spacing (letter & word advance widths + line gap). The preview uses your traced letters — untraced letters show as dashed boxes.
fontmaker.panels.special_intro: Specialized letterforms — auto-composed from your traced letters. The wide letterforms each get a Width slider (it both adds side space and stretches); the dagesh / mapiq forms and yod-with-hiriq compose from your letter plus its mark. Insert them by their Unicode code point.
fontmaker.panels.special_precomposed_hin: Set where the dot sits in the combined glyph (e.g. שׁ / שׂ).
fontmaker.panels.style_title: Pick Bold to export this project as the Bold style of the same family — install the Regular and Bold files together and the B button switches between them.
fontmaker.panels.svg_outline_hint: Imported from SVG — no tracing needed. Fine-tune the shape with Edit points, or re-upload under Add Letters to replace it.
fontmaker.panels.test_combos_tip: Add {combo} to the sample text — hard to type without a nikkud keyboard.
fontmaker.panels.tip_finer_move: Tip: use the arrow keys for finer, exact movement.
fontmaker.panels.trace_base_first: Trace the base letter(s) first to preview this form.
fontmaker.panels.trace_hint: Lower threshold captures lighter ink; higher detail hugs the ink more closely (more nodes). Corners sets how sharp a turn must be to stay a crisp corner — slide right to round more of them into smooth curves. Counters (ס, ם, ע) punch out automatically. Turn on Outline only for hollow “bubble” letters — line weight sets the ring thickness.
fontmaker.panels.trace_under_font: This letter came from a font file, so it's already vectorized — no tracing needed. Go to Nikkud.
fontmaker.panels.trace_under_svg: Imported from SVG — already vectorized. Fine-tune points if you like, then go to Nikkud.
fontmaker.panels.traced_readout_title: Core Hebrew letters with an outline traced
fontmaker.panels.unfinished_btn_title: Jump to the next letter still missing an outline or its anchors (Shift + ], or Shift + [ to go back)
fontmaker.panels.upload_mark_below: Upload an image of this mark below.
fontmaker.panels.version_title: Edit it freely — also ticks up on each export.
fontmaker.panels.wide_auto_hint: Auto-composed from your traced {bases}. The Width slider both adds side space and stretches the outline — saved automatically.
fontmaker.panels.wide_convert_hint: Stretch looking wonky? Convert this form into a real glyph you can edit point by point. It stops following the base letter — you can revert anytime.
fontmaker.panels.wide_edited_hint: Converted to an editable glyph — the exported font ships your edited outline, and this form no longer follows its base letter. Revert to return to the auto-stretched version.
fontmaker.panels.wide_intro: A wide variant of every letter — auto-stretched from your traced letters (150% to start). Pick one to adjust its Width slider, or convert it to an editable glyph if the stretch needs hand-fixing. The exported font includes them at their code points and in the ss02 “Wide letterforms” stylistic set.
fontmaker.panels.wide_nikkud_hint: Vowels on this wide form follow {name}'s placement, stretched to fit — so they stay consistent with the plain letter. Preview one below; to move it, edit the nikkud on {name}.
fontmaker.panels.wide_vowels_follow: This wide form's vowels follow its base letter — size it with the Width slider on the left, and edit the vowel positions on the base letter.
fontmaker.panels.word_spacing_hint: Word spacing is also the width of the Space (U+0020) glyph.
fontmaker.panels.yiddish_intro: Yiddish forms, composed from your traced letters: pasekh / komets alef, the rafe letters (בֿ כֿ פֿ), the vov/yud digraphs (װ ױ ײ), and pasekh tsvey yudn (ײַ).

privacy.header.title: IvritSuite — Privacy Policy
privacy.legal.changes: If this policy is updated, the "Effective date" at the top of the page will change. Material changes will be reflected on this page; there is no mailing list or account to notify because the site does not collect contact information.
privacy.legal.children: IvritSuite is designed to be safely usable by students of all ages, including children under 13. The site does not knowingly collect personal information from any user, regardless of age. There is no account creation, no submission form, no chat, and no upload feature. If you believe any personal information has somehow been collected in violation of this policy, please contact us through the contact page and we will remove it.
privacy.legal.collect: IvritSuite is almost entirely client-side. There are no accounts, no logins, and no submissions, and the site stores no personal data on a server. Specifically: No personal information. The site does not ask for, transmit, or store your name, email address, school, classroom roster, or any other personally identifiable information. Tool content stays in your browser. Anything you create with the tools — worksheet presets, classroom-dashboard schedules and settings, flash-card preferences, dictionary filters, Torah Trainer settings — is stored locally in your browser using the standard localStorage API. It never leaves your device through any channel operated by the site. No tracking pixels or fingerprinting. For aggregate usage statistics the site uses only Google Analytics 4, described in Section 3.
privacy.legal.contact: Questions or concerns about this policy can be directed to Harrison Bleiberg via the contact page, or by email at {email}.
privacy.legal.cookies: The site uses Google Analytics 4 (measurement ID G-CMLC81Z0HC) to understand which tools are used and how visitors arrive at the site. GA4 collects aggregated, anonymized data such as page views, approximate geographic region, device class, and referral source. IP addresses are anonymized by GA4 by default and are not stored by the site operator. You can control or block analytics in several ways: Use your browser's "Do Not Track" or tracking-protection settings. Install the Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on. Block third-party scripts via your preferred ad/tracker blocker. For details on Google's data handling, see Google's Privacy Policy.
privacy.legal.ferpa_analytics: The site's only data collection is anonymized, aggregated Google Analytics 4 usage data (page views, device class, region). GA4 anonymizes IP addresses and is not associated with any student identifier; this data is not directly or indirectly linkable to individual students and therefore does not constitute "education records" or "personally identifiable information" under 34 CFR § 99.3.
privacy.legal.ferpa_designation: Because no PII or education records are disclosed to the site, schools and districts may permit teachers and students to use IvritSuite without entering into a separate data-sharing or "school official" agreement under the FERPA exception at 34 CFR § 99.31(a)(1). If your district nevertheless requires a written acknowledgment of these practices, you may rely on this policy as a public statement of them.
privacy.legal.ferpa_intro: This section is provided for school administrators, IT departments, and educators evaluating IvritSuite for classroom use under the U.S. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA, 20 U.S.C. § 1232g; 34 CFR Part 99).
privacy.legal.ferpa_noads: IvritSuite does not sell, rent, license, or otherwise share any user information with advertisers or data brokers. The site displays no advertising.
privacy.legal.ferpa_norecords: IvritSuite does not collect, receive, store, or transmit any personally identifiable information (PII) from student education records as defined by FERPA. The site has no user accounts, no class rosters, no grade books, no submission of student work, and no server-side storage of teacher- or student-generated content. Worksheets, presets, schedules, and tool preferences are stored exclusively in the local browser using localStorage and remain on the user's own device.
privacy.legal.ferpa_parental: Because no student records are stored by the site, there is nothing for parents to inspect, amend, or have removed under FERPA's parental-rights provisions on the site's side. Parents wishing to review locally stored tool settings can do so directly in the browser used by the student via the home-page Import / Export All Settings control.
privacy.legal.ferpa_questions: For FERPA-specific inquiries, please contact Harrison Bleiberg through the contact page.
privacy.legal.intro: IvritSuite (the "site") is a free collection of Hebrew literacy tools for teachers and students, operated by Harrison Bleiberg. This Privacy Policy explains what information the site collects (and, more importantly, what it does not), how that information is used, and the choices you have. By using the site you agree to the practices described here.
privacy.legal.localstorage: Because all of your settings live only in your browser, you have full control: The Import / Export All Settings button on the home page lets you download a single JSON backup of every tool's data, restore from a backup, or erase everything in one click. Clearing your browser's site data for IvritSuite removes all stored settings and presets. Using a different browser, device, or private/incognito window will give you a fresh, separate set of settings.
privacy.legal.security: The site is delivered over HTTPS. Because no user data is transmitted to a server operated by the site, the primary security boundary is the user's own browser and device. We recommend keeping your browser up to date and using device-level protections appropriate to your setting.
privacy.legal.thirdparty: Some tools fetch or link to third-party content. Visiting or interacting with these resources is governed by their own privacy policies, not by IvritSuite: Kaikki.org — source of the Hebrew word data used in the dictionary and worksheet generator. PocketTorah — chanted-audio source used by the Torah Trainer. Google Fonts — Hebrew and Latin web fonts. Public weather APIs used by the Classroom Dashboard to display current local weather (only the location you enter is sent, in the standard form required to look up a forecast). Web3Forms and hCaptcha — used only if you send a message through the contact page or the "Suggest a Resource" form on the resources page. The information you enter in those forms is passed to Web3Forms solely to deliver the email to the site operator, and the form uses hCaptcha to block automated spam; both process that data under their own privacy policies. Nothing from the form is stored by IvritSuite.

torah.about.faq_a1: A free Hebrew Torah reader. Pick a parsha and read it with optional transliteration, English translation, per-vowel color coding, cantillation strip, prose TTS, and chanted-audio karaoke that highlights words in time with the recording. When you are done reading, copy the passage out as formatted text or print it as a classroom sheet.
torah.about.faq_a2: Yes. PocketTorah's recordings of all 54 parshiyot and haftarot stream on demand, with word-level highlighting synchronized to the audio. Adjust playback speed without re-fetching.
torah.about.faq_a3: Sefaria's public API. The translation dropdown defaults to JPS 1985 when available; pick any other version from the same dropdown.
torah.about.faq_a4: Yes. The Display panel has separate toggles for nikkud (vowel points) and cantillation marks (te'amim). They can be hidden independently.
torah.about.faq_a5: Yes. Trope color coding tints each word by its cantillation clause family — Sof Pasuk, Zakef Katon, Segol, Revia, Geresh, and rare marks — with a legend above the reading. It composes with vowel color coding, keeps working when the cantillation marks themselves are hidden, and each family's color is customizable in settings.
torah.about.faq_a6: The default is diaspora. Flip the Reading Schedule toggle to switch to Israel. Use "Jump to this week's parsha" to auto-pick the current week's reading from Sefaria's calendar.
torah.about.faq_a7: Yes. Materials incorporating PocketTorah audio are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; other IvritSuite content is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
torah.about.faq_a8: Yes. The Copy panel in the Options drawer copies the passage as rich text, keeping the vowel and trope colors, so it pastes into Google Docs, Word, or Pages. Copy one verse, select several, or type a verse range, and choose what travels with it — nikkud, cantillation marks, transliteration, translation, verse numbers, or blank lines for handwriting.

trope.learn.family_note_geresh: Ornamental short phrases: kadma-v'azla (geresh), double gershayim, the telisha twins at the word's edges, and the whirling pazer.
trope.learn.family_note_katon: The workhorse mid-verse clause: mahpach and pashta climb toward zakef katon's little pause. Pashta looks exactly like kadma — only its position at the end of the word gives it away.
trope.learn.family_note_rare: Once-in-a-Torah specialties — mercha kefula, karnei parah, and yerach ben yomo. Karnei parah and yerach ben yomo each appear exactly once, back to back, in Numbers 35:5.
trope.learn.family_note_revia: Gentler pauses: revia hovers above the word like a single gem, while darga and tevir often pair up in a distinctive stair-step figure.
trope.learn.family_note_segol: A grand early pause in long verses: zarka swings up and hands off to segol. Shalshelet — a rare, dramatic chain of notes — stands in for it at the very start of a verse.
trope.learn.family_note_sofpasuk: Home base: the backbone of every verse. Mercha and tipcha lead into etnachta — the deep mid-verse resting point — and the same team walks the second half down to the final sof pasuk cadence.
trope.learn.intro: Trope (te'amim) are the cantillation marks that tell you how to chant the Torah. Each card sketches the mark's melody on a small music staff — a rough picture of how the tune rises and falls, not notes to read. Work through them one clause family at a time, then switch to Drill to test yourself. When you're ready to see them in context, open the companion reader: Torah Trainer →

trope.learn.trope_note_etnachta: The deepest pause inside a verse — the wishbone under the word splits the verse in two.
trope.learn.trope_note_geresh_muqdam: A variant geresh printed earlier in the word; some printed editions use it, but this corpus has no occurrences — so there's no clip to play.
trope.learn.trope_note_kadma: Sits on the stressed syllable, usually leading straight into a geresh ("kadma v'azla"). Same shape as pashta, which instead hangs off the word's end.
trope.learn.trope_note_karnei_parah: "Cow horns" — the single rarest mark; one appearance in the Torah (Numbers 35:5).
trope.learn.trope_note_mahpach: A rising horseshoe below the stressed syllable, almost always followed by pashta.
trope.learn.trope_note_mercha_kefula: A doubled mercha — appears only a handful of times in the whole Torah.
trope.learn.trope_note_pashta: Postpositive — printed at the very end of the word even when the stress falls earlier (it's doubled on the stress in that case). Same shape as kadma; position tells them apart.
trope.learn.trope_note_segol: Postpositive — the three-dot cluster rides off the end of the word.
trope.learn.trope_note_shalshelet: A long, dramatic chain of notes — always on a verse's first word, always followed by a vertical paseq line.
trope.learn.trope_note_sof_pasuk: The verse-ending cadence. Its siluk mark shares a codepoint with the meteg stress line, so learn it by position: the last word of every verse, followed by the ׃ mark.
trope.learn.trope_note_telisha_gedola: Prepositive — the small circle leads the word from the front.
trope.learn.trope_note_telisha_ketana: Postpositive — the small circle sits at the end of the word.
trope.learn.trope_note_yerach_ben_yomo: "Moon one day old" — appears once in the Torah, right before karnei parah's word (Numbers 35:5).
trope.learn.trope_note_yetiv: Prepositive — printed at the very start of the word, below the first letter. Same shape as mahpach, different position and role.
trope.learn.trope_note_zakef_gadol: Zakef katon's louder sibling — a vertical bar joins the two dots when the word stands alone in its clause.
trope.learn.trope_note_zarka: Postpositive — curls off the end of the word and always throws ahead to a segol.
